title: Nice to Caprera: the Sailor, the Two Republics, and the Kingdom He Gave Away
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Ligurian Sea and the Death Sentence

stops.name: Nice, birth in the old port quarter
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Domenico Garibaldi runs coasting vessels out of a port the French Empire has annexed and calls Nice; his wife Rosa Raimondi keeps the house in the quarter behind the quays. Their son Giuseppe Maria is born on the fourth of July into Ligurian speech, Ligurian trade, and a city whose nationality will change twice more before he dies. His mother means him for the priesthood, his father for the law or medicine. He is put instead in the way of the sea, which is what the street outside the door is for.
suggested_refs: The Garibaldi birthplace on the quay at Nice, in the quarter behind the old port
sources: Research pool, geography lens, birthplace entry

stops.name: Genoa, entered among the ship's boys
stops.date_confidence: Date attested. Place corrected: the pool's chronology lens gave the same date but placed the register entry at Nice, while the Italian Wikipedia article on Garibaldi has him entered among the mozzi at Genoa on 12 November 1821, aged fourteen. Genoa is followed here and the contradiction is recorded rather than resolved.
stops.campa: At fourteen he is written into the register of mozzi, the ship's boys, at Genoa. What follows is the ordinary apprenticeship of the western Mediterranean: brigs and tartanes, grain and hides, quarantine, weather, the Black Sea run. He learns to load fast, to sail short-handed, and to put armed men ashore where nobody is watching. His first documented voyage sails on the thirteenth of January 1824 aboard the Costanza under Angelo Pesante, north through the Bosphorus to Odessa. He is sixteen.
suggested_refs: The Genoese register of mozzi, 12 November 1821
The Costanza under Angelo Pesante, Genoa to Odessa, January 1824
sources: Lucy Riall, Garibaldi: Invention of a Hero (2007)

stops.name: Taganrog, the schooner Clorinda
stops.date_confidence: Month and year attested. The identification of the shipmate who converts him, traditionally Giovanni Battista Cuneo, is flagged in the pool as not beyond doubt; the day is unknown and defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: In a port at the shallow end of the Sea of Azov, loading for the grain trade, the twenty-five-year-old mate of the Clorinda falls in with a passenger who talks politics. The talk is Mazzini's: one Italy, a republic, made by the people and granted by no king. Garibaldi has crossed and recrossed the Mediterranean for a decade with no idea in his head beyond a berth and a wage. He goes ashore at Taganrog a sailor and comes back aboard a conspirator. Who did it is traditionally given as Giovanni Battista Cuneo, and the record does not quite close on that.
suggested_refs: The Italian merchant community of Taganrog on the Sea of Azov, 1833
sources: Research pool, geography lens, Taganrog entry, which flags the Cuneo identification as uncertain

stops.name: Genoa, sworn to Young Italy as Cleombroto
stops.date_confidence: Month and year attested; day unknown, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Back in Genoa he seeks out Mazzini and takes the oath of Young Italy, choosing the conspiratorial name Cleombroto after the Spartan king who marched out knowing he would not come back. To be useful he enlists in the Royal Sardinian Navy, meaning to carry the rising into the fleet from below. In February 1834 the Piedmont insurrection collapses before it begins. Garibaldi, waiting at his post for a signal that never comes, deserts and goes to ground. A Sardinian military tribunal tries him in his absence and sentences him to death.
suggested_refs: The Young Italy oath and the Genoa naval conspiracy of February 1834
The Sardinian military tribunal's sentence of death in absentia, 1834
sources: Research pool, chronology lens, entries for November 1833 and February 1834

stops.name: Marseille, out of reach of the sentence
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Nine days after the collapse he is in Marseille, twenty-six years old and condemned in a country he can no longer enter. He works passages out of the Vieux Port, and the exile that begins here will run twelve years. He owns no property and holds no rank, and his living is one he can pick up in any harbour in the world. In 1835 he takes a berth for Rio de Janeiro, where a rebel province is at war with an empire and is looking for men who can handle a boat.
suggested_refs: The Vieux Port of Marseille, first refuge of the twelve-year exile
sources: Research pool, geography lens, Marseille entry

segments.name: The Southern Cross: the Farrapos and Anita

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro, the exile meets Bento Goncalves
stops.date_confidence: Canonical pin inherited byte-identical from anita_garibaldi.journey.json, which corroborates the Rio meeting with Bento Goncalves from the Portuguese and English Wikipedia articles on Anita Garibaldi and the Guerra dos Farrapos. Day and month unknown, defaulted to 01. The pool's chronology lens dated his enlistment to 1835; that is the war's start year, and the letter of marque is dated 4 May 1837 in the Italian article.
stops.campa: In the Brazilian capital the Italian exiles keep a shop and a printing habit, and through them Garibaldi reaches Bento Goncalves da Silva, president of the breakaway Riograndense Republic, and asks for a commission. On the fourth of May 1837 he is given a letter of marque as first lieutenant of the vessel Mazzini, named for the man whose oath he swore in Genoa. He is a privateer now, in a war between a rebel province and an empire. He has never sailed this coast. The republic that commissions him holds no port worth the name.
suggested_refs: The letter of marque of the Riograndense Republic, 4 May 1837
The vessel Mazzini, Garibaldi's first command

stops.name: Gualeguay, hung by the wrists
stops.date_confidence: The pool's geography lens dates the Gualeguay imprisonment to 1837 without a month; June is placed here only to order the segment after the letter of marque of 4 May. The torture is carried from the dossier and was not independently corroborated in the research pass, nor was it found anywhere else in the atlas.
stops.campa: Taking prizes under a commission no other government recognises, he is caught in Argentine waters and handed to the authorities at Gualeguay in Entre Rios. He is held there months and, by his own later account, strung up by the wrists from a beam and left hanging when he will not name his accomplices. He gets away on horseback with a guide, is retaken, gets away again. The account is his own. No Argentine record has been produced either to confirm it or to contradict it.
suggested_refs: Garibaldi's memoir account of the Gualeguay imprisonment, in the Dumas and Dwight recensions
sources: Research pool, geography lens, Gualeguay entry, drawn from the dossier chapter 'First exile and Brazil'

stops.name: Laguna, the woman on the shore
stops.date_confidence: Canonical pin and date inherited byte-identical from anita_garibaldi.journey.json. The telescope scene and the line 'Devi essere mia' are flagged there and in this pool as retrospective legend built on a documented meeting, not witnessed courtship; the pool's chronology lens dates the partnership from October 1839 aboard the Rio Pardo, which is not the same event as the meeting.
stops.campa: Laguna falls to the Farrapos and is declared the capital of a second breakaway state, the Catarinense republic. Garibaldi comes ashore into a town four months old and finds Ana Maria de Jesus Ribeiro, eighteen, married to a shoemaker who has gone for a soldier. She leaves with him. The retelling has him picking her out through a ship's telescope and announcing, in Italian she cannot yet understand, that she must be his; the retelling is his own, written years afterward, and nobody else was standing there. Anita Garibaldi learns to ride armed and to work a gun aboard the Rio Pardo.
suggested_refs: Garibaldi's memoir, Dwight translation 1861, ch. IX, and the Dumas-edited Vita e memorie of 1860, on the meeting at Laguna
sources: Research pool, afterlife lens, entry flagging the telescope scene as legend

stops.name: Curitibanos, the wife lost in the retreat
stops.date_confidence: Canonical pin and date inherited byte-identical from anita_garibaldi.journey.json. The pool's chronology lens carries the defeat as tag R, noting it was not independently re-verified from a fetched source; the ride out through the lines is flagged as tradition in Anita's own file.
stops.campa: The Imperial navy retakes Laguna in November and the republican column breaks southwest into the sertao with the cavalry of the empire behind it. At Curitibanos it is caught. Anita, pregnant, is taken and separated from him; she asks leave to search the field and turns the dead over one at a time until she has established that her husband is not among them. Then, by a tradition the record keeps as tradition, she takes a horse and rides out through the lines. Garibaldi hears nothing for days and learns she is alive from a rider on the road.
suggested_refs: The Farroupilha retreat of January 1840 through the Santa Catarina highlands
sources: Research pool, chronology lens, Curitibanos entry, tagged R

stops.name: Mostardas, the birth of Menotti
stops.date_confidence: Date and place corrected. The pool's chronology lens gave an undated 1840 with Porto Alegre coordinates about 130 km away; the Italian Wikipedia article on Menotti Garibaldi gives 16 September 1840 at the borough of Sao Luis, now part of Mostardas. The quotation's own passage dates the sheltering to September 1840 at San Simon, which the pool's quote lens had mislabelled as a Uruguayan episode.
stops.campa: The republic they fight for is losing and the column lives off what it can drive. Between marches Anita is brought to a house on the coastal plain and bears a son, named Domenico Menotti for the Modenese conspirator hanged by the Duke of Modena in 1831; the child carries a dent in his skull from a fall his mother took during the retreat. Garibaldi is a beaten privateer with no ship, no pay, and now a family. Decades later, dictating his memoir, he writes down exactly what he owes the people who took them in.
stops.quote: Saro reconoscientissimo, a quella buona gente, tutta la mia vita
stops.quote_source: Garibaldi on the household that sheltered Anita at San Simon, Rio Grande do Sul, September 1840, in Theodore Dwight, trans., 'The Life of General Garibaldi' (New York, 1859), Project Gutenberg ebook 50544
suggested_refs: The house at San Simon, Rio Grande do Sul, where Anita was sheltered in September 1840
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 50544, Dwight, The Life of General Garibaldi

stops.name: Montevideo, married at San Francisco
stops.date_confidence: Date attested. The legal status of Anita's first marriage is disputed among biographers and the dossier itself records that Garibaldi represented the first husband as dead; the dispute is left open here.
stops.campa: They drive a herd overland to Montevideo, arrive with roughly half of it, sell the hides, and take a rented room in the Ciudad Vieja. He teaches mathematics for a season and works as a commercial broker, badly. On the twenty-sixth of March they are married in the church of San Francisco, Garibaldi having stated that Anita's first husband is dead. Whether that was true, and whether the first marriage was ever validly dissolved, biographers still argue over. Four children are born to them. Three live.
suggested_refs: The marriage register of the church of San Francisco, Ciudad Vieja, Montevideo, 26 March 1842
sources: Research pool, geography lens, Montevideo marriage entry

stops.name: Costa Brava, the squadron burned on the Parana
stops.date_confidence: River and province corrected. The pool's geography lens placed this at -32.2, -58.4, on the Uruguay river near Concepcion del Uruguay; the Combate de Costa Brava of 15 and 16 August 1842 was fought on the Parana at the Entre Rios and Corrientes boundary near Esquina. The coordinates approximate the river reach, not a landmark.
stops.campa: Commanding three small vessels for the Montevidean government, he is run down on the Parana by Guillermo Brown, the Irish-born admiral of Rosas's Argentine fleet, and fought to a standstill across two days. Out of powder and out of river, Garibaldi lands his crews, takes off what a man can carry, and burns his own ships to the waterline rather than let Brown tow them away. It is his first command of a squadron. He walks the survivors out through Corrientes.
suggested_refs: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combate_de_Costa_Brava, 15 and 16 August 1842
sources: Research pool, geography lens, Costa Brava entry with correction

stops.name: Montevideo, the Italian Legion and the red shirts
stops.date_confidence: The pool's chronology lens compressed two events into 1842. Command of the Uruguayan fleet belongs to 1842; the Legione italiana was formed in the spring of 1843 and Garibaldi took command of it, per the Italian Wikipedia article, at the end of that year. December is used only to order the stop. Pin inherited from sarmiento.journey.json and benigno_villanueva.journey.json.
stops.campa: Oribe's army sits down outside Montevideo for what becomes a siege of nine years, and inside the walls the city arms whatever it has: French residents, freed slaves, Argentine exiles, and some five hundred Italians. Garibaldi takes the Italian Legion at the end of 1843. Their uniform is an accident of the market. A Montevideo warehouse is holding a lot of red woollen shirts made for the slaughterhouses of Buenos Aires, unsold because the trade has stopped, and the Legion is issued them at a price the treasury can meet.
suggested_refs: The Legione italiana of Montevideo and the origin of the red shirt
sources: Research pool, chronology lens, 1842 entry with correction

stops.name: San Antonio del Salto, the day the name carries
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Some two hundred of the Legion, caught in the open near Salto by a force many times their number, hold a walled enclosure through an afternoon and break out at night carrying their wounded. In military terms it is a successful escape. Montevideo strikes a decoration for it. Subscription committees in Genoa, Milan, and London take the story up and print it across Europe. The sword of honour voted him is sold and the money given to the widows of the men who did not come out.
stops.quote: There is not time enough; and we must fight.
stops.quote_source: Garibaldi to Baez, who had proposed retreating before a much larger force, in Theodore Dwight, trans., 'The Life of General Garibaldi' (New York, 1859), Project Gutenberg ebook 50544
suggested_refs: The action at San Antonio del Salto, 8 February 1846, and the Montevidean decoration struck for it
sources: Research pool, geography lens, San Antonio entry
Project Gutenberg ebook 50544, Dwight, The Life of General Garibaldi

segments.name: The Roman Republic and the Retreat

stops.name: Milan, the volunteer command
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; month placed to order the segment. The pool's chronology lens attached the founding of the Partito d'Azione to this return; that is false as dated, since Mazzini founded the party in March 1853 and the Italian Wikipedia article lists Garibaldi among its leading figures but not as a founder.
stops.campa: He lands at Nice on the twenty-first of June aboard the Speranza, bought by subscription from the Italian community of Montevideo, and offers his sword to Charles Albert of Sardinia, the king whose tribunal condemned him to death fourteen years earlier. The king has no use for him. The provisional government of Lombardy does, and gives him a volunteer command in a war Piedmont has already lost. He goes on fighting after the armistice, wins a skirmish at Luino on Lake Maggiore, and is pushed over the Swiss frontier with a handful of men.
suggested_refs: The Speranza, purchased by subscription at Montevideo for the return of 1848
The action at Luino, August 1848
sources: Research pool, geography lens, Nice and Milan and Luino entries

stops.name: Rome, the first French assault thrown back at Porta San Pancrazio
stops.date_confidence: Date attested. Coordinate corrected: the pool's geography lens gave 41.8944, 12.4636, about 700 m north of the gate, while the Italian Wikipedia article places Porta San Pancrazio at 41.8883, 12.4614.
stops.campa: Pius IX has fled to Gaeta, a constituent assembly has proclaimed the Roman Republic, and a French expeditionary force under Oudinot lands at Civitavecchia to put the Pope back. On the thirtieth of April Oudinot marches up on the Janiculum expecting the gates to be opened for him. Garibaldi's legionaries and the students of the city meet him at the wall and in the villas outside it and drive him back toward the coast with several hundred prisoners taken. Garibaldi wants to pursue and destroy the column. Mazzini, governing, forbids it, unwilling to make war on a sister republic.
suggested_refs: Porta San Pancrazio and the Villa Corsini, ground of the fighting of 30 April and June 1849
sources: Research pool, geography lens, Porta San Pancrazio entry with correction

stops.name: Rome, out through the Lateran with four thousand
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction between four dates, recorded and not resolved. The pool's chronology lens gave 1 July for the withdrawal; the English Wikipedia article on the Roman Republic gives 2 July for the march out and 3 July for the French entry; the Italian article dates the formal dissolution to 4 July. The Assembly vote to end resistance falls on 1 July. The march out is dated here to 2 July.
stops.campa: The siege has run a month. Oudinot comes back with thirty thousand men and siege artillery, takes the Janiculum bastions by assault, and shells the city over the heads of its defenders. On the first of July the Assembly votes to end resistance. The next day Garibaldi forms up in the square before San Giovanni in Laterano and marches out with some four thousand who choose to follow him rather than take the terms, turning north for Venice, the last republic still holding. The French enter Rome on the third. Anita rides in the column, pregnant, her hair cut short.
suggested_refs: The Piazza San Giovanni in Laterano, assembly point of the column of 2 July 1849
sources: Research pool, chronology lens, entries for 29 June and 1 July 1849 with correction

stops.name: San Marino, the column dissolves at the wall
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Four Austrian armies, a Spanish force, and the Neapolitans quarter the peninsula between them, and the column loses men at every march. At the end of July what is left of it comes under the walls of the little republic, whose authorities negotiate safe conduct on condition that the men disband. Garibaldi releases them from their oath and says he is going on. Two hundred or so go with him down to the Adriatic at Cesenatico, where they seize thirteen fishing bragozzi and put to sea for Venice with the Austrian navy patrolling the coast.
suggested_refs: The safe conduct negotiated by the Republic of San Marino, 31 July 1849
The seizure of the bragozzi at Cesenatico, 1 August 1849
sources: Research pool, geography lens, San Marino entry

stops.name: Mandriole, Anita dies at the Guiccioli farm
stops.date_confidence: Date and hour attested. Coordinate corrected: three lenses of the research pool gave three different points, all between 9 and 11 km too far south, one of them falling on the Capanno Garibaldi in the Ravenna pineta, a different site two days later in the escape. The Italian Wikipedia article places Mandriole at 44.5540, 12.2213. Later stories of strangulation or poisoning lack documentary support.
stops.campa: The boats are taken or driven ashore; Garibaldi lands near the Po delta with Anita dying and Austrian patrols working the lagoons behind him. Guides pass the pair from farm to farm across the marsh. At the Fattoria Guiccioli near Mandriole she is carried in and laid on a bed, and at a quarter to eight on the evening of the fourth of August she dies in his arms. He is got away within hours. She is buried in the sand in a hurry. A dog digs the body up. It is reburied, and over the next eighty-three years it will be exhumed and moved again.
suggested_refs: The Fattoria Guiccioli at Mandriole
The Capanno Garibaldi in the Ravenna pineta, refuge of 6 August 1849, often confused with the Guiccioli farm
sources: Research pool, chronology and geography and afterlife lenses, all three with divergent coordinates

segments.name: The Second Exile: Tallow, Guano, Coal

stops.name: Rosebank, Staten Island, the candle factory
stops.date_confidence: Arrival date attested. Canonical New York pin inherited byte-identical from ettore_ferrari.journey.json, which anchors it at 420 Tompkins Avenue, Rosebank; the pool's chronology and geography lenses gave two coarser Staten Island points.
stops.campa: New York meets the ship with a committee and a plan to parade him. He refuses it, is laid up for weeks with rheumatism, and then goes to live in a cottage at Rosebank on Staten Island with Antonio Meucci, a Florentine exile boiling tallow into candles. Garibaldi dips wicks and works the vats. Meucci is at the same time building the apparatus he will later claim as a telephone, and the story that the two men developed it together is Italian-American embroidery that no document supports. In October he writes to a New York editor and sends him, first of all, a life of his wife.
stops.quote: According to what I have promised you, I send you the first biographical sketch; and do not be surprised that it is that of my wife. She was my constant companion, in good and bad fortune, sharing, as you will see, my greatest dangers, and surpassing the bravest men.
stops.quote_source: Garibaldi to Theodore Dwight, Staten Island, 30 October 1850, printed in Theodore Dwight, trans., 'The Life of General Garibaldi' (New York, 1859), Project Gutenberg ebook 50544
suggested_refs: The Garibaldi-Meucci house at 420 Tompkins Avenue, Rosebank, Staten Island
Ettore Ferrari's 1923 memorial to Antonio Meucci at the same cottage
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 50544, Dwight, The Life of General Garibaldi
Research pool, geography lens, Staten Island entry

stops.name: Canton, the Carmen in the Pacific trade
stops.date_confidence: Month and year from the pool's geography lens; the chronology lens dates the sailing from Callao to 10 January 1852. Day unknown, defaulted to 01. The allegation that this voyage carried indentured Chinese labour is carried forward from the dossier as unverified: no manifest, port record, or cargo document was produced in the research pass, and it sits badly with his documented abolitionist correspondence.
stops.campa: Unable to get an American command, he crosses Central America, reaches Callao, and takes the merchant ship Carmen for a Peruvian house in the guano trade. The circuit runs Callao to Canton and home by the Philippines and Australia. He is a working shipmaster again at forty-five, on the far side of the world from any Italian question, keeping a log and arguing with agents about freight. An accusation trails this voyage through the literature, that the Carmen carried indentured Chinese labourers, and nothing in any shipping record has been produced to settle it either way.
suggested_refs: Peruvian and Chinese shipping records of the coolie trade, early 1850s, for the unresolved allegation against the Carmen
sources: Research pool, afterlife lens, unverified coolie-transport entry, tagged R

stops.name: South Shields, the Tyne crowds
stops.date_confidence: Month and year attested; day unknown, defaulted to 01. He ends the exile at Genoa on 10 May 1854, a few weeks after leaving the Tyne.
stops.campa: Commanding the Commonwealth out of Baltimore he puts into the Tyne for coal and stays a month. Word gets round the yards and the pits, and the working men of Tyneside come down to the wharf; the local radicals talk Italy at him for hours at a stretch. He is a ship's captain in his forties with a death sentence behind him and no country, six years short of Sicily and not yet the figure of 1860. The pitmen and the shipwrights subscribe for him anyway. What they hand over is an inscribed sword and a telescope.
suggested_refs: The sword and telescope presented to Garibaldi by the working men of Tyneside, March and April 1854
sources: Research pool, geography lens, South Shields entry

stops.name: Caprera, half an island bought with a dead brother's money
stops.date_confidence: Year corrected to 1855. The pool's chronology lens gave 1854 and its geography lens '1855 onward'; the Italian Wikipedia article on Caprera fixes the purchase of the northern half of the island to 1855 and to the inheritance from his brother Felice, who died that year. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Amnestied and back in Italy, he buys the northern half of a granite island off the Sardinian coast with money his brother Felice left him: scrub, wind, goats, and a spring. He builds a low white house in the South American manner, plants vines and olives, walls fields out of stone he clears himself, and works them. For the next twenty-seven years visitors from London and Paris will come ashore expecting a general and find a farmer in a poncho with dirt to the wrist. He keeps a boat drawn up on the beach below the house.
suggested_refs: The Casa Bianca and farm at Caprera, in the Maddalena archipelago
sources: Research pool, geography lens, Caprera entry with correction

stops.name: Varese, the Hunters of the Alps
stops.date_confidence: Battle date attested. The quotation belongs to the manifesto he issued on resigning his central Italian command later the same year; it is placed here because the campa carries the stop through to that resignation.
stops.campa: Cavour, wanting Austria provoked and the volunteers kept out of the regular army's way, makes Garibaldi a major general and hands him three thousand men without artillery or cavalry: the Cacciatori delle Alpi. He takes them into Lombardy ahead of the main armies, beats the Austrians at Varese on the twenty-sixth of May and at San Fermo three days after, and is in Como before the week is out. Villafranca stops the war half finished in July. Ordered to stand down in central Italy that autumn, he resigns his command and writes to the men he is leaving.
stops.quote: For you, as for me, the greatest of all possible misfortunes would be not to be present wherever there is fighting for Italy. Young men who have sworn to be faithful to Italy and to the chief who will lead you to victory, lay not down your arms; remain firm at your post.
stops.quote_source: Garibaldi, manifesto 'To My Companions in Arms in Central Italy,' on resigning his command, 1859, in Theodore Dwight, trans., 'The Life of General Garibaldi' (New York, 1859), Project Gutenberg ebook 50544
suggested_refs: The Cacciatori delle Alpi of 1859 and the actions at Varese, San Fermo, and Como
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 50544, Dwight, The Life of General Garibaldi

stops.name: Fino Mornasco, a marriage of one morning
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He marries Giuseppina Raimondi, eighteen, daughter of the marchese who guided his column through the Alpine foothills the year before. As the wedding party comes out of the chapel a letter is put into his hand: the bride is pregnant by an officer of his own volunteers. Garibaldi asks her whether it is true. She does not deny it. The marriage is never consummated and the annulment will take twenty years. He leaves within the hour, fifty-two years old, and never sees her again.
suggested_refs: The annulment proceedings of the Raimondi marriage, concluded 1879
sources: Research pool, chronology lens, Fino Mornasco entry

stops.name: Quarto, the two steamers taken in the night
stops.date_confidence: Date attested for the night of 5 to 6 May. Coordinate corrected: the pool's chronology lens gave 44.3989, 9.0233, about 2.6 km inland toward Quinto, and its geography lens 44.3908, 9.0086. The Italian Wikipedia article places the Scoglio di Quarto embarkation point at 44.3892, 8.9919. The atlas holds a Quarto pin of 44.418, 8.98 in dannunzio.journey.json for the 1915 speech at the monument; it is not inherited here because the verified embarkation coordinate is the better anchor for Garibaldi's own stop.
stops.campa: A rising in Palermo has been put down, the reports coming out of Sicily contradict one another, and Cavour will neither authorise the expedition nor stop it. On the night of the fifth of May a little over a thousand volunteers, most of them northerners, a great many of them students, lawyers, and doctors, gather on the rocks below the Villa Spinola at Quarto. Two Rubattino steamers, the Piemonte and the Lombardo, are taken by an arrangement everyone involved denies afterward. They carry about a thousand old muskets and no artillery.
suggested_refs: The Scoglio di Quarto and the monument to the Thousand, site of the embarkation of 5 May 1860
Gabriele D'Annunzio's Discorso di Quarto at that monument, 5 May 1915

stops.name: Marsala, the landing under British guns
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: They come in at Marsala on the eleventh with two Bourbon warships closing behind them. Two British vessels are lying in the harbour to protect the English wine houses, and the Bourbon gunners hold their fire long enough for the volunteers to get ashore dry. That is the whole of the British intervention: a hesitation of perhaps an hour. The version in which Palmerston delivered Sicily to Garibaldi has been told for a century and a half and rests on this and nothing else. The Lombardo grounds and is abandoned. By evening the expedition is on Sicilian soil and has lost nobody.
suggested_refs: The Marsala wine houses of Woodhouse and Ingham and the British vessels in the harbour, 11 May 1860
sources: Research pool, geography lens, Marsala entry

stops.name: Calatafimi, the hill called Pianto Romano
stops.date_confidence: Battle date attested. The quotation is a veteran's retrospective account written forty-four years later, not a transcript: Giuseppe Cesare Abba, who was there as a boy of twenty, prints it in 1904, and the Italian Wikipedia article on the battle judges the phrase probably attributable to Risorgimento rhetoric. The pool tags it R and the tag stands, with Abba named as the earliest traceable source rather than the phrase being called untraced.
stops.campa: At Salemi the day before, he assumed the dictatorship of Sicily in the name of Victor Emmanuel, a formula that turns a filibuster into a government. Now two thousand Bourbon regulars hold a terraced hillside above the road and the volunteers have to climb it, terrace by terrace, into the fire, with bayonets and thrown stones. They take it in the late afternoon. Nino Bixio, beside him and hit, says the position cannot be carried, and gets an answer the survivors will still be repeating in 1904.
stops.quote: Qui si fa l'Italia o si muore.
stops.quote_source: Reported as said to Nino Bixio at Calatafimi, 15 May 1860, in Giuseppe Cesare Abba, 'Storia dei Mille' (1904), ch. 'Dopo la vittoria,' p. 129, it.wikisource.org
suggested_refs: The hill of Pianto Romano above Calatafimi
Giuseppe Cesare Abba, Storia dei Mille (1904), earliest traceable source for the phrase

stops.name: Palermo, in through the Porta Termini
stops.date_confidence: Date corrected. The pool's chronology lens gave 21 June 1860, which matches no standard date for the city; the English Wikipedia article on the Expedition of the Thousand has Garibaldi's forces entering on 27 May, street fighting from 28 to 30 May, and the Bourbon garrison capitulating on 6 June. The entry date is used here.
stops.campa: Twenty thousand Bourbon troops hold Palermo. Garibaldi feints inland toward Corleone, doubles back along a mountain track, and comes at the city from the southeast before dawn, breaking in at the Porta Termini with the Sicilian squadre behind him. The population rises and builds barricades in its own streets. The royal fleet in the bay shells the city for three days. On the sixth of June the garrison capitulates. Twenty thousand men march down to the transports and are shipped out of Sicily.
suggested_refs: The Porta Termini and the barricades of Palermo, 27 to 30 May 1860
The capitulation of the Bourbon garrison, 6 June 1860
sources: Research pool, geography lens, Palermo entry with correction

stops.name: Bronte, five men shot under the dictatorship
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Sicilian peasants have read the revolution as a promise of land. At Bronte on the western slope of Etna, in an estate the British crown gave to Nelson, they rise, burn the town hall, and kill sixteen people. Garibaldi sends Nino Bixio, who declares martial law, convenes a tribunal that sits a few hours, and has five men shot the same day, among them the lawyer Nicolo Lombardo, who had tried to hold the crowd back. The dictatorship does not review the sentences. Sicily goes north into the new kingdom with its estates intact.
suggested_refs: The Bronte executions of 10 August 1860 and the Nelson estate at Maniace
sources: Research pool, geography lens, Bronte entry, from the dossier section 'Land, order, and Bronte'

stops.name: Naples, entering by train
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He crosses the Strait of Messina on the nineteenth of August, lands in Calabria at Melito di Porto Salvo, and walks up the length of the kingdom in three weeks against an army that will not fight him. Francis II leaves Naples for the fortress at Gaeta. Garibaldi arrives by train from Vietri with a few staff officers, drives through streets packed to the walls, past Bourbon gun crews standing to their pieces who present arms as he passes, and takes possession of a capital of half a million people without a shot fired.
stops.quote: To-morrow, Victor Emanuel, the king of Italy, the elect of the nation, will cross the line which has divided us from the rest of our country for so many centuries... No more political distinctions! no more parties! no more discords! Italy one.
stops.quote_source: Garibaldi, 'Proclamation of Garibaldi to the Inhabitants of Naples,' October 1860, in Theodore Dwight, trans., 'The Life of General Garibaldi,' Project Gutenberg ebook 50544
suggested_refs: The Melito di Porto Salvo landing, 19 August 1860
The Palazzo Reale and the Naples proclamations of September and October 1860
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 50544, Dwight, The Life of General Garibaldi

stops.name: The Volturno, the largest battle of the campaign
stops.date_confidence: Date corrected to 1 October 1860. The pool's chronology lens gave 30 September, following the English Wikipedia article on Garibaldi; the article on the Battle of the Volturno dates the action to 1 October, with skirmishing the previous day and a second day of mopping up, and gives coordinates 41.0919, 14.0944. The geography lens's 1 October governs here.
stops.campa: The Bourbon army has not been destroyed. It has fallen back behind the Volturno on Capua and Gaeta with fifty thousand men and its guns, and on the first of October it comes out. Twenty-four thousand volunteers hold a line twenty miles long from the sea to Maddaloni through a day of separate battles, and Garibaldi spends it moving between them by carriage and on horseback. They hold, and a second day goes in mopping up. It is the only pitched battle of his career fought at the head of an army rather than a raiding column.
suggested_refs: The Volturno line from Santa Maria Capua Vetere to Maddaloni, 1 and 2 October 1860
sources: Research pool, geography lens, Volturno entry with correction

stops.name: Teano, the handover on the road
stops.date_confidence: Date traditional and generally accepted; the exact site, the wording, and whether he was first to hail Victor Emmanuel as king of Italy are disputed in the sources and heavily ritualised in later accounts. The pool flags all three as unresolved.
stops.campa: Piedmontese regulars have invaded the Papal States from the north to put themselves between the volunteers and Rome, and the two armies meet on a road outside Teano. Garibaldi rides up, takes off his hat, and hails Victor Emmanuel as king of Italy; the king answers, by most accounts, coldly. Whether the words were those words, and whether it happened at the bridge or the crossroads or a mile further on, is disputed by nearly everyone who claimed to have been standing there. He hands over the south, twenty-two million people, and asks for nothing.
suggested_refs: The disputed site of the Teano meeting, 26 October 1860, and its later monumental fixing
sources: Research pool, geography lens, Teano entry, drawn from the dossier's Myths section

stops.name: Caprera, the sack of seed corn
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The new kingdom offers him a dukedom, a castle, the rank and pension of a general, a dowry for his daughter. He refuses all of it. His volunteers are absorbed or dismissed without his being asked to review them, and the officers he commissioned find their ranks disputed for years. The steamer that carries him home on the ninth of November carries also a sack of seed corn, some coffee and sugar, and a bundle of dried fish. Before he sails he issues a proclamation to the men he raised.
stops.quote: To arms all! all! and the oppressors, the supremely powerful, shall be turned into dust.
stops.quote_source: Garibaldi, proclamation 'To My Companions in Arms,' on retiring to Caprera, November 1860, in Theodore Dwight, trans., 'The Life of General Garibaldi,' Project Gutenberg ebook 50544
suggested_refs: The proclamation to his companions in arms, November 1860
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 50544, Dwight, The Life of General Garibaldi
Research pool, chronology lens, 9 November 1860 entry

segments.name: Rome or Death, and the American Republic

stops.name: Aspromonte, shot by Italian soldiers
stops.date_confidence: Date attested. The wound is corrected: the pool's geography lens gave only 'shot in the right foot', while the English Wikipedia article on the battle records two bullets, one in the hip and one in the malleolus of the right ankle.
stops.campa: Two years after handing over a kingdom he raises volunteers in Sicily under the cry Roma o morte, crosses to Calabria, and marches for Rome, which Napoleon III's garrison holds for the Pope. The government he made declares him a rebel and sends the regular army against him. In the pines of the Aspromonte he orders his men not to fire on Italian soldiers; a few fire anyway, briefly, and are stopped. Two bullets hit him, one in the hip, one in the ankle. He is carried down the mountain on a stretcher, a prisoner of the state he handed over.
suggested_refs: The Piani d'Aspromonte, 29 August 1862
sources: Research pool, geography lens, Aspromonte entry with correction

stops.name: Varignano, the prisoner offers himself to Lincoln
stops.date_confidence: Letter date attested from the text printed by H. Nelson Gay in 1907. Varignano is the fort where he was held from September; the extraction of the ball did not happen here, see the Pisa stop.
stops.campa: He is held in the naval fort at Varignano near La Spezia with the ball still in his ankle, and Europe sends surgeons to argue over it. The year before, agents of Abraham Lincoln's government had come to Caprera to offer him a major general's commission in the Union army; he had answered that he could not come at present, and privately that he would not fight except under supreme command and for an explicit act of emancipation. Now, sixteen days after Italian troops shot him, the American consul climbs the stairs of the fort and puts the question again.
stops.quote: Sir: I am a prisoner and severely wounded: in consequence it is impossible for me to dispose of myself. However, I believe that, if I am set at liberty and if my wounds heal, the favorable opportunity will have arrived in which I shall be able to satisfy my desire to serve the great American Republic, of which I am a citizen, and which to-day combats for universal liberty.
stops.quote_source: Garibaldi to United States Consul Theodore Canisius, Varignano, 14 September 1862, in H. Nelson Gay, 'Lincoln's Offer of a Command to Garibaldi,' The Century Magazine 75:1 (November 1907), archive.org item lincolnsofferofc00gayh
suggested_refs: The Varignano fort near Porto Venere
The 39th New York Volunteer Infantry, nicknamed the Garibaldi Guard, raised in his honour without his participation
sources: archive.org item lincolnsofferofc00gayh, H. Nelson Gay, Lincoln's Offer of a Command to Garibaldi
battlefields.org, Giuseppe Garibaldi and President Lincoln

stops.name: Pisa, the ball drawn out at the Tre Donzelle
stops.date_confidence: Place corrected. The pool's geography lens set the extraction at Varignano, the fort where he was imprisoned from September; the Italian Wikipedia article on Ferdinando Zannetti has Zannetti removing the ball at ten in the morning of 23 November 1862 at Pisa, where Garibaldi was lodged at the Albergo delle Tre Donzelle. The instrument is corrected too: Nelaton's probe was porcelain-knobbed, not electromagnetic.
stops.campa: Amnestied and moved to Pisa, he lies in a room at the Albergo delle Tre Donzelle for eleven weeks while consultants from three countries disagree about whether there is a ball in the ankle at all. Auguste Nelaton sends up a probe of his own design tipped with porcelain, which comes out marked with a grey smear of lead. On the morning of the twenty-third of November, Ferdinando Zannetti opens the joint and lifts the ball free. The wound has been open since August and the leg will never carry him properly again.
suggested_refs: Nelaton's porcelain-tipped probe, devised for this case
Ettore Ferrari's bronze Garibaldi for Pisa, 1892, in the Piazza Garibaldi

stops.name: Caprera, the letter to the great emancipator
stops.date_confidence: Date attested; the manuscript is in the Library of Congress, Abraham Lincoln Papers, Series 1, General Correspondence. The pool tagged this quotation R for want of an archival citation and the citation has since been traced. The English text's translator is not named by the source that reproduces it, so the manuscript record is cited alongside.
stops.campa: The Emancipation Proclamation has taken effect on the first of January, which is the condition he set in 1861 and was not given. From Caprera, an island he farms with his own hands, he writes to Washington, and his sons Menotti and Ricciotti sign the letter under his name. Beside Christ he names John Brown, hanged at Charles Town in December 1859 for trying to arm slaves out of a federal arsenal and three and a half years dead when the letter is written.
stops.quote: Posterity will call you the great emancipator, a more enviable title than any crown could be, and greater than any merely mundane treasure. You are a true heir of the teaching given us by Christ and by John Brown.
stops.quote_source: Giuseppe, Menotti and Ricciotti Garibaldi to Abraham Lincoln, 6 August 1863; manuscript in the Library of Congress, Abraham Lincoln Papers, Series 1, loc.gov/item/mal2537500/; English text as reproduced by the American Battlefield Trust
suggested_refs: The Garibaldi letter of 6 August 1863 in the Abraham Lincoln Papers, Library of Congress

stops.name: London, the crowds and the shortened tour
stops.date_confidence: Month and year attested; day unknown, defaulted to 01. The entry into London falls on 11 April and the departure on 28 April. The government's stated reason for the curtailment was his health; the dossier and the pool both read it as concern about public order.
stops.campa: He lands at Southampton and comes into London on the eleventh of April through half a million people; the carriage takes six hours to cross the city. He is received by the Prince of Wales, dines with Palmerston, is given the freedom of the City, and sees Mazzini, whom the ministry would rather he did not see. Working men's committees plan him a tour of the industrial north. Gladstone and the cabinet decide it has gone far enough, and a physician is produced who finds that his health requires him to go home. He sails on the twenty-eighth.
suggested_refs: The London reception of April 1864 and the cabinet's curtailment of the northern tour
sources: Research pool, geography lens, London entry, from the dossier chapter 'London apotheosis, Freemasonry, and the 1866 war'

segments.name: The Last Wars and the Granite

stops.name: Bezzecca, the telegram of one word
stops.date_confidence: Battle date attested; the telegram is dated 9 August 1866 and is placed in this stop because it belongs to the same campaign. Coordinate corrected: the pool's geography lens gave 45.8367, 10.7889, roughly 8 to 9 km southeast in the mountains toward Lake Garda, and its chronology lens 45.85, 10.7333; the Italian Wikipedia article places Bezzecca at 45.8970, 10.7183. The telegram is widely attested but was not re-fetched from a primary text in the research pass.
stops.campa: Italy goes to war beside Prussia and loses at Custoza and again at Lissa. The volunteers, forty thousand of them now and given the worst ground on the map, are the one Italian force that takes anything: wounded at Monte Suello in early July and directing from a carriage afterward, Garibaldi sees them nearly broken in the Val di Ledro on the twenty-first and then take Bezzecca, and the road to Trento is open. Then Vienna makes its peace with Berlin, and the kingdom is ordered to hand the Trentino back. Told to withdraw, he wires one word.
stops.quote_source: Garibaldi's telegram to General La Marmora on being ordered to evacuate the Trentino after the armistice, 9 August 1866
suggested_refs: The Val di Ledro and the field of Bezzecca, 21 July 1866
The Obbedisco telegram, 9 August 1866
sources: Research pool, geography and chronology lenses, Bezzecca entries with coordinate correction

stops.name: Geneva, the Congress of Peace and Freedom
stops.date_confidence: Canonical pin and date inherited byte-identical from mikhail_bakunin.journey.json. That file places Victor Hugo and John Stuart Mill on the League's committee; whether Hugo attended the 1867 congress in person, as against lending his name and a letter, is not established by the sources reachable in this pass and is left open.
stops.campa: Six thousand people fill the Palais Electoral for the founding congress of the League of Peace and Freedom, and Garibaldi opens it as honorary president with twelve propositions, among them that the papacy is the most harmful of all sects and that every religion should give way to reason. Victor Hugo and John Stuart Mill are on the committee. Mikhail Bakunin comes to the tribune meaning to take the League for anarchism and is applauded for it. Garibaldi leaves within days for the frontier of the Papal States with a rifle in the carriage.
suggested_refs: The Palais Electoral, Geneva, and the founding congress of the League of Peace and Freedom, September 1867
sources: Research pool, geography lens, Geneva entry

stops.name: Mentana, the Chassepots
stops.date_confidence: Date attested. Canonical pin inherited byte-identical from blavatsky.journey.json; the pool's geography lens gave 42.0122, 12.7358, about 7 km east in open country, and its chronology lens 42.0333, 12.6667. Blavatsky's presence in the ranks rests on her own later account and is not independently documented.
stops.campa: The volunteers have taken Monterotondo and are working down toward a Roman rising that does not come. At Mentana the papal zouaves are stiffened by a French expedition landed at Civitavecchia three days earlier, carrying the new breech-loading Chassepot, which outranges everything the volunteers have and decides the day from a distance at which they cannot answer. The line breaks. Among the wounded left on the field, by her own account given years afterward, is Helena Blavatsky, dragged out alive with her arm and her leg broken.
suggested_refs: The French report on the Chassepot at Mentana, 3 November 1867
Blavatsky's account of her wounds at Mentana

stops.name: Autun, the Army of the Vosges
stops.date_confidence: Canonical pin and date inherited byte-identical from ettore_ferrari.journey.json. The pool's geography lens dates the Dijon operations to November 1870 and gives 47.322, 5.0415 for Dijon; this stop covers the winter headquarters and the Dijon fighting together, and the day is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Napoleon III falls at Sedan, the republic proclaimed in Paris asks for volunteers, and Garibaldi, sixty-three and barely able to walk, sails for France to fight for the country whose soldiers shot at him at Mentana and threw him out of Rome twice. He is given the Army of the Vosges: twenty thousand foreigners and francs-tireurs nobody else wants. He holds Autun through the winter and fights round Dijon, where his men take a Pomeranian regimental colour, the only German flag captured in the whole war. Ettore Ferrari serves that winter as the Italian government's liaison to his headquarters.
suggested_refs: The Pomeranian colour taken at Dijon, January 1871
Ettore Ferrari's Garibaldi Series in bronze and marble, 1892 onward
sources: Research pool, geography lens, Dijon entry

stops.name: Bordeaux, shouted out of the Assembly
stops.date_confidence: Canonical Bordeaux pin inherited byte-identical from victor_hugo.journey.json, which dates Hugo's own resignation over a Garibaldi motion to 13 March 1871. The pool's geography lens dates Garibaldi's own scene to February 1871; 13 February is used here for his resignation and the Hugo sequel is dated in the campa by month only.
stops.campa: Four French departments elect him to the National Assembly meeting at Bordeaux. When he rises the monarchist majority, which has just lost a war and blames the republic for it, howls him down and disputes whether a foreigner may sit at all. He resigns his seat and leaves the same day. Victor Hugo defends him from the tribune, is shouted down in his turn over the same question, and resigns his own seat in March. Garibaldi goes back to Caprera. He does not leave Italy again.
suggested_refs: The Bordeaux sitting of the National Assembly, February and March 1871
Victor Hugo's speech and resignation over the Garibaldi question
sources: Research pool, geography lens, Bordeaux entry

stops.name: Caprera, the granite and the unburnt body
stops.date_confidence: Death date attested. The coordinate is the afterlife lens's pin for the Casa Bianca and the family cemetery, marginally different from the geography lens's 41.2075, 9.446 for the same compound; the discrepancy is recorded, not resolved. The funeral falls on 8 June 1882. The unfulfilled cremation request is tagged R in the pool, agreed by Treccani and the Sardinian regional museum service.
stops.campa: He dies in the white house on the second of June, seventy-four years old, crippled with arthritis, married since 1880 to Francesca Armosino, who had come to the island as his children's nurse. His will of 1881 asks that he be burned on a pyre of acacia and myrtle and that a handful of the ashes go under a juniper. The government and the family decline. Six days later, with ministers and generals and delegations of veterans standing in the scrub, he is put in the ground under a rough unworked block of granite, in sight of the fields he cleared himself.
suggested_refs: The family cemetery at Caprera and the granite tomb
The Compendio Garibaldino di Caprera, opened as a museum in 1976
The Museo Nazionale Memoriale Giuseppe Garibaldi in the Arbuticci fortress, reopened 2012
